Published online:
    August 31, 2026

Geographic focus:
    United States (Middle East as secondary context)

Temporal focus:
    T1. Historical report [NO]
    T2. Forward-looking reporting short-term risks (next few weeks/months) [YES]
    T3. Forward-looking reporting long-term risks (next quarters/years) [NO]

Synopsis:
    US equity futures fell on Aug 31 as US-Iran military strikes pushed oil prices higher, stoking inflation fears. Fed Chair Kevin Warsh's hawkish Jackson Hole debut the prior week effectively eliminated near-term rate cut expectations. Markets are now pricing a >60% probability of a September rate hike (up sharply from 41.4% a week prior). Energy stocks bucked the selloff while utilities led declines. Key near-term catalyst is the September 4 jobs report, which could further cement or complicate the Fed's next move.

Q01. Is the content's main message on the US economy, US yields, US interest rates?
Relevance: YES (the article centers on Fed rate hike expectations, inflation dynamics, and their impact on US equity markets)

Q02. Is the content about increasing US interest rates?
Relevance: 90 (strongly focused on rate hike probability, Warsh's hawkish tone, and BofA's view that a hike is now the base case)
Probability of increase: 60%+ (as per CME FedWatch, up from 41.4% a week ago)

Q03. Is the content about holding stable US interest rates?
Relevance: 15 (holding is mentioned only implicitly as the alternative if Sept 4 jobs data surprises to the downside)
Probability of holding: ~40% (implied residual from the >60% hike probability)

Q04. Is the content about decreasing US interest rates?
Relevance: 5 (rate cuts explicitly taken off the table by Warsh per the article)
Probability of decrease: ~0% (Warsh's remarks removed any near-term cut probability)

Q05. Focus on the very latest information: What is the sentiment/tone including the very latest information on US interest rates?
Sentiment: 80 (materially more hawkish — Warsh's Jackson Hole address eliminated cut expectations, hike probability surged to >60%, and geopolitical-driven oil inflation adds further upward pressure on rates; only uncertainty is the Sept 4 NFP print)
